blocks.p: Now the old Recorder and my Lord Understanding, with some others of the chief men of the town (those, that is, who knew they must stand or fall with the famous town of Mansoul), met together one day, and after consulting, agreed jointly to draw up a petition and send it to Emmanuel while he sat in the gate of Mansoul. So they drew up their petition to Emmanuel, and its contents were these:
We, the old inhabitants of the now pitiable town of Mansoul, confess our sin, and are sorry that we have offended your princely Majesty; and we pray that you will spare our lives.

He gave no answer at all to this petition, and that troubled them all the more. Meanwhile the captains in the Recorder’s house kept the battering-rams at work on the gates of the castle, to beat them down. So after some time, labor, and toil, the castle gate that was called Impregnable was beaten open and broken into splinters, and a way was made up to the stronghold where Diabolus had hidden himself. Then word was sent down to Ear-gate, where Emmanuel still remained, that a way had been made in at the castle gates. But oh, how the trumpets sounded throughout the Prince’s camp at the news, for now the war was so near its end, and Mansoul so near to being set free!
Then the Prince rose from where he was, took with him those of his men of war who were best suited for that expedition, and marched up the street of Mansoul to the old Recorder’s house.

Now the Prince himself was clad all in armor of gold, and so he marched up through the town with his standard carried before him; but all the way he kept his face very reserved, so that the people could not tell from his looks whether to read love or hatred in them. As he marched up the street, the townsfolk came out of every door to see, and could not help being taken with his person and its glory; but they wondered at his reserve, for as yet he spoke to them more by his actions and works than by words or smiles. And poor Mansoul, as everyone in such cases is apt to do, read Emmanuel’s bearing toward them the way Joseph’s brothers read his toward them: exactly the wrong way round. “For,” they thought, “if Emmanuel loved us, he would show it to us by word or bearing; but he does neither, so Emmanuel hates us. And if Emmanuel hates us, then Mansoul will be slain; then Mansoul will become a dunghill.” They knew that they had broken his Father’s law, and that they had sided against him with Diabolus, his enemy. They also knew that Prince Emmanuel knew all this; for they were convinced that he was like an angel of God, knowing all things that are done on the earth. And this made them think their condition was miserable, and that the good Prince would make them desolate.

“And,” they thought, “what time could be more fitting for it than now, when he holds the bridle of Mansoul in his hand?” And I took special notice of this: in spite of all this, the inhabitants could not, no, they could not, as they watched him march through the town, keep from cringing, bowing, bending, and being ready to lick the dust off his feet. They wished a thousand times over that he would become their Prince and Captain, and their protection. They would talk to one another about how handsome he was, and how far he outshone the great ones of the world in glory and valor. But, poor hearts, when it came to themselves, their thoughts would swing about and run to every kind of extreme. Yes, with their thoughts working backward and forward, Mansoul became like a ball tossed about, like a rolling thing before the whirlwind.

Now when he came to the castle gates, he commanded Diabolus to come out and surrender himself into his hands. But oh, how loath the beast was to come out! How he balked at it! How he shrank! How he cringed! Yet out he came to the Prince. Then Emmanuel gave the command, and they took Diabolus and bound him fast in chains, the better to keep him for the judgment Emmanuel had appointed for him. But Diabolus stood up to plead for himself, begging Emmanuel not to send him into the deep, but to let him leave Mansoul in peace.

When Emmanuel had taken him and bound him in chains, he led him into the marketplace, and there, before Mansoul, stripped him of the armor he had boasted of so much before. This was one of Emmanuel’s acts of triumph over his enemy; and all the while the giant was being stripped, the trumpets of the golden Prince sounded loud, the captains shouted, and the soldiers sang for joy.
Then Mansoul was called on to see the beginning of Emmanuel’s triumph over the one in whom they had trusted so much, and of whom they had boasted so much in the days when he flattered them.

Having made Diabolus naked in the eyes of Mansoul and before the Prince’s commanders, he next ordered that Diabolus be bound with chains to his chariot wheels. Then he left some of his forces, namely Captain Boanerges and Captain Conviction, as a guard for the castle gates, so that there would be resistance on his behalf if any of Diabolus’s former followers should try to seize it; and he rode in triumph over him right through the town of Mansoul, and so out by the gate called Eye-gate, to the plain where his camp lay.
But unless you had been there, as I was, you cannot imagine what a shout there was in Emmanuel’s camp when they saw the tyrant bound by the hand of their noble Prince and tied to his chariot wheels!

And they said, “He has led captivity captive [Eph. 4:8]; he has stripped principalities and powers. [Col. 2:15] Diabolus is brought under the power of his sword, and made the object of everyone’s scorn.”

Those who rode as volunteers, too, who had come down to see the battle, shouted with such a great voice and sang with such melodious notes that they made those who live in the highest spheres open their windows, put out their heads, and look down to see the cause of all that glory.

The townsmen also, as many as saw this sight, were, as it were, hanging between earth and heaven while they watched. True, they could not tell how things would turn out for themselves; but everything was done in such excellent order that, I cannot tell how, the whole proceeding seemed to cast a smile toward the town; so that their eyes, their heads, their hearts, their minds, and all they had were caught and held as they watched Emmanuel’s order.

So when the brave Prince had finished this part of his triumph over Diabolus his foe, he turned him out in the midst of his contempt and shame, with a charge never again to be the possessor of Mansoul. Then Diabolus went away from Emmanuel and out from the middle of his camp, to inherit the parched places in a salt land [Jer. 17:6], seeking rest but finding none. [Matt. 12:43]

Now Captain Boanerges and Captain Conviction were both men of very great majesty. Their faces were like the faces of lions, and their words like the roaring of the sea; and they were still quartered in Mr. Conscience’s house, which I mentioned before. So when the high and mighty Prince had finished his triumph over Diabolus this far, the townsmen had more leisure to watch these noble captains. But the captains carried themselves with such terror and dread in everything they did (and you may be sure they had private instructions to do so) that they kept the town in continual heartache, and made the future well-being of Mansoul, as the townsmen saw it, hang in doubt before them; so that for a considerable time they did not know what rest, or ease, or peace, or hope meant.

Nor did the Prince himself live in the town of Mansoul yet, but in his royal pavilion in the camp, among his Father’s forces. So at a convenient time he sent special orders to Captain Boanerges to summon all the townsmen of Mansoul into the castle yard, and there, before their faces, to take my Lord Understanding, Mr. Conscience, and that notable one, the Lord Willbewill, and put all three under arrest, and to set a strong guard over them there until his pleasure concerning them was further known. When the captains carried out these orders, it added not a little to the town’s fears; for now, as they thought, their earlier fears of Mansoul’s ruin were confirmed. What death they would die, and how long they would be in dying, was what most perplexed their heads and hearts. Yes, they were afraid that Emmanuel would command them all into the deep, the place that the prince Diabolus himself was afraid of; for they knew they had deserved it. And to die by the sword in the sight of the town, in open disgrace, at the hand of so good and so holy a prince: that troubled them sorely too. The town was also greatly troubled for the men under arrest, because they were its support and its guides, and because they believed that if those men were cut off, their execution would be only the beginning of the ruin of the town of Mansoul. So what did they do but, together with the men in prison, draw up a petition to the Prince, and send it to Emmanuel by the hand of Mr. Would-live. So he went, and came to the Prince’s quarters, and presented the petition, the substance of which was this:
Great and wonderful Ruler, victor over Diabolus and conqueror of the town of Mansoul:

We, the miserable inhabitants of that most woeful town, humbly beg that we may find favor in your sight. Remember against us neither our former transgressions nor the sins of the chief men of our town; but spare us according to the greatness of your mercy, and let us not die, but live in your sight. Then we will be willing to be your servants, and, if you see fit, to gather our food under your table. Amen.

So the petitioner went with his petition to the Prince, as I said; and the Prince took it from his hand, but sent him away in silence. This still distressed the town of Mansoul; but considering that now they must either petition or die, since there was nothing else they could do, they consulted again and sent another petition, much in the same form and manner as the first.

But when the petition was drawn up, the next question was, who should take it? They would not send this one by the man who had taken the first, for they thought the Prince had taken some offense at the way he had conducted himself before him. So they tried to make Captain Conviction their messenger; but he said that he neither dared nor would petition Emmanuel for traitors, or be an advocate for rebels before the Prince. “And yet,” he said, “our Prince is good, and you may venture to send it by the hand of one of your own townsmen, provided he goes with a rope around his head and pleads nothing but mercy.”

Well, out of fear they put it off as long as they could, and longer than was good for them; but fearing at last the danger of delay, they decided, with many a sinking of heart, to send their petition by Mr. Desires-awake. So they sent for him. He lived in a very poor cottage in Mansoul, and he came at his neighbors’ request. They told him what they had done and meant to do about petitioning, and that they wanted him to take it to the Prince.

Then Mr. Desires-awake said, “Why shouldn’t I do the best I can to save so famous a town as Mansoul from the destruction it deserves?” So they handed him the petition, told him how he must address the Prince, and wished him ten thousand good speeds. So he came to the Prince’s pavilion, as the first messenger had, and asked to speak with his Majesty. Word was carried to Emmanuel, and the Prince came out to the man. When Mr. Desires-awake saw the Prince, he fell flat with his face to the ground and cried out, “Oh, that Mansoul might live before you!” And with that he presented the petition. When the Prince had read it, he turned away for a while and wept; but restraining himself, he turned back to the man, who all this while lay crying at his feet as at first, and said to him, “Go your way to your place, and I will consider your requests.”

Now you may imagine how those of Mansoul who had sent him, what with guilt and what with fear that their petition would be rejected, looked out many a long look, with strange stirrings of heart, to see what would become of it. At last they saw their messenger coming back. When he arrived, they asked him how he had fared, what Emmanuel had said, and what had become of the petition. But he told them he would keep silent until he came to the prison, to my Lord Mayor, my Lord Willbewill, and Mr. Recorder. So he went on toward the prison house where the men of Mansoul lay bound. But oh, what a crowd flocked after him to hear what the messenger would say! When he arrived and showed himself at the prison gate, my Lord Mayor himself turned as white as a sheet, and the Recorder shook as well. But they asked him, “Come, good sir, what did the great Prince say to you?”

“When I came to my Lord’s pavilion,” said Mr. Desires-awake, “I called, and he came out. So I fell flat at his feet and handed him my petition; for the greatness of his person and the glory of his face would not let me stay on my feet. As he took the petition, I cried, ‘Oh, that Mansoul might live before you!’ And when he had looked at it a while, he turned around and said to his servant, ‘Go your way to your place again, and I will consider your requests.’” The messenger added, “The Prince you sent me to is such a one for beauty and glory that whoever sees him must both love and fear him. For my part, I can do no less. But I do not know what the end of these things will be.”

At this answer they were all at a standstill, both those in prison and those who had followed the messenger there to hear the news; nor did they know what sense, or what kind of sense, to make of what the Prince had said. Now when the prison was cleared of the crowd, the prisoners began to comment among themselves on Emmanuel’s words. My Lord Mayor said the answer did not wear a harsh face; but Willbewill said it boded evil; and the Recorder, that it was a messenger of death. Now those left standing at the back, who could not hear the prisoners well, caught one piece of a sentence and a bit of another; some took hold of what the messenger had said, and some of the prisoners’ judgment on it; so none of them understood things rightly. But you cannot imagine what a commotion these people made, and what confusion there was in Mansoul now.

For at once those who had heard went flying about the town, one crying one thing and another the exact opposite; and both were sure they were telling the truth, for they had heard it with their own ears, they said, and so could not be mistaken. One would say, “We must all be killed”; another would say, “We must all be saved”; a third would say that the Prince would have nothing to do with Mansoul; and a fourth, that the prisoners were to be put to death immediately. And, as I said, every one insisted that his own tale was the right one, and that everyone else was wrong. So Mansoul now had trouble upon trouble, and no one knew where to rest the sole of his foot. For if a man passing by heard his neighbor telling his tale, he would be sure to tell the exact opposite, and each would insist he had the truth. Some of them had even got hold of the story that the Prince intended to put Mansoul to the sword. And now it began to grow dark, so poor Mansoul was in sad perplexity all that night until the morning.

But as far as I could gather from the best information I could get, all this uproar came from what the Recorder had said when he told them that, in his judgment, the Prince’s answer was a messenger of death. It was this that set the town on fire and began the fright in Mansoul; for in former times Mansoul had been used to regarding Mr. Recorder as a seer, and his judgment as equal to that of the best of orators. And so Mansoul was a terror to itself.

And now they began to feel what came of stubborn rebellion and unlawful resistance against their Prince. I say, they now began to feel its effects in the guilt and fear that had now swallowed them up; and who was more caught up in the one than those who had been most deeply in the other, namely, the chief men of the town of Mansoul?
